{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=self-determination+theory+and+cognitive+offloading+framework+in+competitive+sports+AI+adoption&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.5841722\", \"title\": [\"Cognitive Divergence Theory of AI Adoption\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5841722\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7270039\", \"title\": [\"PAUSE: A Privacy-preserving Self-reflection Tool for AI-associated Cognitive Offloading\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Cognitive offloading is the use of external aids, such as notes, calculators, or search engines, to reduce mental effort. Large language models (LLMs) extend this to thinking itself, and by AI-associated cognitive offloading, I mean the pattern where a person routinely substitutes LLM output for their own reasoning, idea generation, learning, or communication. Recent empirical work reports associations between some patterns of LLM use and changes in critical thinking effort, neural engagement during assisted tasks, creative diversity, learning behaviour, and social dependence. Validated instruments for AI reliance, dependence, and literacy have begun to appear. I describe PAUSE (Patterns of AI Use: Self-Examination) , a privacy-by-design web tool that occupies a different niche from these. It is a lightweight, non-diagnostic reflection aid for private individual use. PAUSE is organised around how a person's own LLM use may relate to cognitive offloading across four everyday domains (reasoning &amp; critical thinking, creativity &amp; originality, research &amp; learning, and social &amp; communicative capacity). It delivers a short, free, no-login self-check, scores it entirely in the browser, and returns descriptive, domain-aware reflections. The self-check pairs reverse-scored behavioural items with a claim-evaluation reasoning probe, an alternative-uses creativity probe, and a small retrospective before-and-after block. PAUSE does not assume that AI use is harmful. It addresses the narrower case where AI substitutes for effort a person may want to preserve. The application is privacy-preserving by design: scoring is deterministic and runs client-side, no personal data is required, nothing is transmitted or stored beyond the browser session, and no LLM is involved in production. In this paper, I describe the conceptual grounding, the item design, the scoring, the architecture, and the design philosophy. PAUSE is a self-reflection tool, not a validated psychological instrument. It presents no reliability or validity evidence, and all readings should be interpreted as descriptive self-reflection rather than psychological measurement.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7270039\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6669899\", \"title\": [\"Cognitive Offloading and the Erosion of Authentic Self-Reflection in AI-Assisted Mental Health Practices\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p><p><span>Artificial Intelligence is increasingly being used in mental health practices, particularly in activities such as journaling and emotional reflection. While these tools improve accessibility and help individuals articulate their thoughts, they also raise concerns about the authenticity of self-reflection. This paper examines how AI-assisted reflection may influence emotional processing through the concept of cognitive offloading, where individuals rely on external systems to perform mental tasks. It argues that while AI can support individuals in organizing their thoughts, over-reliance on these tools may reduce cognitive effort and limit deeper emotional engagement. The paper proposes a conceptual framework suggesting that AI-assisted reflection can lead to reduced effort, which may weaken emotional processing and self-awareness over time. It concludes that AI should function as a support system rather than a replacement for human reflection.</span></p></jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6669899\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6548138\", \"title\": [\"A Framework for Measuring Human Cognitive Agency Amid Routine AI Adoption\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The rapid integration of large language models into everyday cognitive tasks writing, reasoning, decision-making, and professional judgmenthas created an urgent need for frameworks that capture the cognitive consequences of delegating thinking to AI systems. Existing constructs in psychology and education, including critical thinking, metacognition, intellectual autonomy, and epistemic agency, each address related phenomena but none adequately describes the specic capacity threatened by habitual AI-assisted cognition: the ability to remain the genuine author of one's own understanding. This paper introduces cognitive sovereignty as a distinct psychological construct, dened as the capacity to (a) notice when one's thinking is being displaced (b) maintain a meaningful connection to how one's beliefs and judgments are formed, and (c) distinguish between genuine reasoning and the subjective impression of having reasoned. I trace the concept's philosophical lineage, dierentiate it from adjacent constructs through systematic comparison, propose a ve-dimensional model (Authorship Awareness, Process Ownership, Source Discrimination, Capacity Maintenance, and Delegation Discernment), present a nomological network with predicted relations to existing measures, and outline a measurement instrument: the Cognitive Sovereignty Scale (CSS), with candidate items and a multi-phase validation strategy. We conclude with specic, testable predictions that follow from the framework. We argue that cognitive sovereignty names a phenomenon that existing constructs individually fail to capture and that its operationalization is a prerequisite for empirical research on the cognitive consequences of AI adoption.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6548138\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "42d47ebba3a498781e91b840f0b808e94947d3700bf17d1d263ae0f6aecfdbe7", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "emergent_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.5841722", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7270039", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6669899", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6548138"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5841722", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7270039", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6669899", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6548138"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
